hints: Notice the reagent, KOH dissolved in ethanol means elimination, not substitution, so J loses HBr to form a C=C double bond.
List all the possible C4H8 alkenes first, remembering that but-2-ene can exist as two stereoisomers, cis and trans.
Ask which bromobutane can eliminate in two different directions to give both but-1-ene and but-2-ene, with the but-2-ene counting as two.
walkthrough:
**Identify the reaction type**

Great start, ethanolic KOH is the classic clue for dehydrohalogenation. A bromoalkane loses $\text{HBr}$ to form an alkene.

$$\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br} + \text{KOH (ethanolic)} \rightarrow \text{C}_4\text{H}_8 + \text{KBr} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Count all possible C4H8 isomers**

For formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$, the structural alkenes are but-1-ene $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, but-2-ene $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$, and 2-methylpropene $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2$. Crucially, but-2-ene shows cis-trans (E/Z) stereoisomerism, so it counts as two distinct isomers.

**Test 2-bromobutane for three products**

Look at $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Removing H from C1 gives but-1-ene. Removing H from C3 gives but-2-ene, which forms as both cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene. That is 1 + 2 = 3 isomeric alkenes, exactly what is observed.

options.A: 1-bromobutane, CH3CH2CH2CH2Br, can only lose H from C2. It gives only but-1-ene, so just one alkene, not three.
options.B: 2-bromobutane, CH3CHBrCH2CH3, is correct. Loss of H from C1 gives but-1-ene, loss of H from C3 gives but-2-ene as a pair of cis and trans stereoisomers. Total is three isomeric C4H8 alkenes.
options.C: 1-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH3)2CHCH2Br, can only lose H from the central C2 to give 2-methylpropene, (CH3)2C=CH2. Only one alkene product is possible.
options.D: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH3)3CBr, is tertiary with three identical methyl groups. Elimination can only give 2-methylpropene, so only one alkene, not three.
